answer:
The bubble-point pressure is about 96.4 kPa (0.951 atm, about 723 mmHg).

Water and n-hexane are practically immiscible. So a 50/50 liquid at 60 °C is two liquid layers, each nearly pure. Each layer exerts its full pure-component vapour pressure, regardless of the overall 50/50 split. The bubble point is reached when the total pressure equals the sum:

P_bubble ≈ P_sat(water) + P_sat(n-hexane)

I computed both vapour pressures at 60 °C two ways, and the two agree to within 0.1 kPa:

| Component | CoolProp (reference equation of state) | Antoine equation |
|---|---|---|
| Water | 19.95 kPa | 19.87 kPa |
| n-Hexane | 76.41 kPa | 76.39 kPa |
| Sum = P_bubble | **96.36 kPa** | 96.26 kPa |

- **Vapour at the bubble point:** about 79 mol% n-hexane and 21 mol% water (y_hexane = 76.4/96.4).
- **Mistake to avoid:** applying Raoult's law as if the liquid were one ideal solution gives 0.5 × 96.4 ≈ 48 kPa. That is wrong by a factor of two, because the two liquids do not mix.
- **Not computed:** I took the two layers as pure. In reality each holds a trace of the other, which would lower the answer slightly. Those trace amounts are tiny (n-hexane dissolves in water at only parts per million), so I expect the effect to be negligible, but I did not compute it.

One consequence of this physics: at about 1 atm (101.3 kPa) the mixture would boil a few degrees above 60 °C. That is well below the normal boiling points of hexane (69 °C) and water (100 °C).

No files were created.
